Highway 88 · Carson Pass · The Sierra Nevada

The Kit Carson Story

A runaway Missouri saddler's apprentice who could not read a book became the guide who helped lead Frémont's expedition on the first recorded U.S. winter crossing of the Sierra — and left his name on the pass above Amador County.

1809 – 1868Frémont ExpeditionsWinter 1844Carson Pass · 8,574 ft

A modern highway through the high Sierra granite country Carson crossed on horseback and on foot, in snow many feet deep. The road is Highway 88 today — in 1844 there was no road at all.

If you live in Fiddletown, you already live in Kit Carson's country. Drive east on Highway 88 — past Cook's Station and Ham's Station, past Kirkwood, Silver Lake and Caples Lake — and the road climbs to a granite saddle at 8,574 feet. The sign at the top says Carson Pass. It is not named for a general or a president. It is named for a scout.

Christopher “Kit” Carson was small, quiet, soft-spoken, and — by most accounts — illiterate. He signed his name with difficulty and had his letters read to him. What he could do, better than almost anyone alive in the 1840s, was read country: water, grass, snow, tracks, weather, and people. He spoke English, Spanish, French, and several Native languages, and he learned sign language fluently. In an era before maps of the West existed, men like Carson were the map.

This is the story of how he got there, of the ambitious young officer who hired him — John Charles Frémont — and of the desperate February weeks in 1844 when the two of them, against explicit warnings, took a party of men straight into the Sierra Nevada in the middle of winter and lived to tell about it.

Chapter One

Two very different men

History often pairs them as “Frémont and Carson,” but they came from opposite ends of American life — and each supplied exactly what the other lacked.

Christopher “Kit” Carson

1809–1868 · The Guide

Born on Christmas Eve 1809 in Kentucky and raised on the Missouri frontier, Carson ran away at about sixteen from a saddler's apprenticeship in Franklin, Missouri, and joined a trade caravan to Santa Fe. A reward notice for the runaway famously offered one cent.

He spent the next fifteen years as a trapper and mountain man — with Ewing Young's party to Arizona and California in 1829–30, then through the Rockies in the 1830s as the beaver trade boomed and collapsed. He hunted for Bent's Fort, learned the languages and customs of the peoples whose country he crossed, and built a reputation in a world where reputation was survival: steady, honest, unflappable, and lethal only when he had to be.

Portrait: Kit Carson in later life. Photo via Library of Congress tradition / public-domain portrait.

John Charles Frémont

1813–1890 · The Pathfinder

Born in Savannah in 1813, Frémont was a brilliant, restless officer in the U.S. Army's Corps of Topographical Engineers — a surveyor with a gift for instruments, botany, and self-promotion. In 1841 he married Jessie Benton, daughter of Senator Thomas Hart Benton of Missouri, the Senate's most powerful voice for westward expansion.

Frémont could measure a mountain. What he could not do was live off an unknown country or find a way through it in winter. For that he needed a guide. In the summer of 1842, aboard a Missouri River steamboat, he met Carson — and hired him on the spot for his first expedition to the Rockies. It was the most consequential hiring decision of both men's lives.

Portrait: John C. Frémont as a young officer and explorer.

“Mounted on a fine horse, without a saddle, and scouring bareheaded over the prairie, Kit was one of the finest pictures of a horseman I have ever seen.”
— John C. Frémont, on first seeing Carson ride

Chapter Two

The expeditions that mapped a continent

In the early 1840s, the United States effectively ended at the Missouri River. Beyond it lay a West known through trappers' tales, a few trails, and blank space on the maps. Congress — pushed by Senator Benton — wanted that blank filled in: routes for emigrants, sites for forts, and knowledge of Oregon and Mexican California. Frémont's expeditions were how it got done, and Carson was at the center of the first three.

Follow the journey west

Tap each stop. This is the arc of the 1843–44 expedition — the long way around, and then the gamble straight over the Sierra.

The first expedition, in 1842, reached South Pass in present-day Wyoming — the great gentle gateway through the Rockies that emigrant wagons would use. The second, in 1843–44, was far more ambitious: out the Oregon Trail, down the Columbia, then south along the eastern flank of the Cascades and Sierra into the Great Basin, a closed desert world of interior rivers that Frémont's party helped prove did not flow to the sea.

Frémont's official reports — shaped into vivid narrative with Jessie's help in Washington — were published by Congress and read all over the country. Emigrants literally carried them west in their wagons. And in those reports, one name kept appearing whenever the party was lost, hungry, or in danger: Kit Carson. A scout who had never sought attention was becoming, without knowing it, a national figure.

Chapter Three · The Centerpiece

February 1844: straight into the wall of snow

By late January 1844, the expedition was in trouble. The party — about two dozen men, with horses, mules, and heavy surveying equipment — had come down the eastern side of the Sierra to the valley that still bears Carson's name. Provisions were running low. The original plan had been to find a pass far to the south. Instead, camped in Carson Valley on January 31, 1844, Frémont made the decision that defines the story: turn west, cross the Sierra now, in midwinter, and resupply at Sutter's Fort in California's Sacramento Valley.

The Washoe people, whose homeland this was — and whose trading route over the mountains had been used for thousands of years — told them plainly not to go. Winter crossings were not done. The snow was too deep, the cold too severe, and there would be nothing for the animals to eat. Frémont recorded the warnings, and went anyway.

What followed was not a dash. It was a month-long grind:

  1. Jan 31, 1844

    The decision in Carson Valley

    Low on food, Frémont turns west toward Sutter's Fort. On the river flowing east out of Hope Valley, he bestows a name that sticks: the Carson River, for his guide.

  2. Early Feb

    Into the snow

    The party follows the Washoe route up toward the crest. Men on snowshoes break trail for the animals; horses flounder and are dug out; instruments and baggage are hauled, abandoned, and hauled again. Snow in the pass country is later described at up to twenty feet deep.

  3. Feb 14, 1844

    A first sight of Tahoe

    Frémont and cartographer Charles Preuss climb Red Lake Peak. From the summit they become the first men of European descent known to have seen Lake Tahoe spread out to the north — a moment of triumph in the middle of a survival march.

  4. Feb 20–21

    Over the crest

    After a final push up the flanks around Red Lake Peak, the expedition clears the summit country of what is now Carson Pass, west of Red Lake. Starving, the men have resorted to eating pack animals — and, in the expedition's own accounts, dogs — to stay alive.

  5. Mar 6, 1844

    Sutter's Fort

    The party descends the western slope — down toward the South Fork American River country, through foothills not far, in spirit, from today's Amador County — and reaches Sutter's Fort. Every man made it. No fatalities. In winter Sierra terms, that alone was extraordinary.

Why Carson mattered in those weeks

Frémont commanded, measured, and wrote. Carson kept them alive and moving: scouting ahead for any line the animals could follow, judging snow and weather, hunting when there was anything to hunt, and dealing with the Native peoples they met in languages he actually spoke. Expedition histories note a nuance worth keeping: Thomas Fitzpatrick was the party's officially engaged guide on paper, and Washoe knowledge pointed the way to the pass itself. Carson's legend grew in the telling — but his competence in that crossing was real, and Frémont knew exactly who he owed.

A tree at the pass later bore a carving — “Kit Carson 1844.” Whether Carson cut it in 1844, or on a later crossing in 1853 when he drove some 6,500 sheep over the pass to sell in gold country, no one can say for certain. The inscribed section was cut from the tree in 1888 and is preserved at Sutter's Fort. The summit is California Historical Landmark No. 315.

Chapter Four

The world they were crossing into

To understand the crossing, you have to un-know modern California. In February 1844, almost nothing a Californian takes for granted existed yet.

California was Mexican

Alta California was a remote province of Mexico, governed from Monterey, populated by a few thousand Californios on ranchos, mission communities in decline after secularization, and — by far the largest population — Native peoples whose lands all of this was. Sutter's Fort, the expedition's goal, was a Swiss immigrant's private trading empire at what is now Sacramento.

No gold rush. No state. No map.

Gold would not be discovered at Sutter's Mill — in Coloma, just over the Amador County line in spirit and a short drive in fact — until January 1848, four years later. There was no California statehood (1850), no railroad over the Sierra (1869), no Highway 88. The Frémont reports were quite literally creating the map emigrants would follow.

An empire arguing with itself

The United States was in the grip of expansion fever — “Manifest Destiny” was about to get its name (1845). Texas annexation, the Oregon boundary dispute with Britain, and war with Mexico were all converging. Frémont's surveying was science, but it was also strategy: every pass he measured was a future road for an expanding republic.

The fur trade was ending

Carson's first world — beaver trapping, rendezvous, Bent's Fort — was collapsing as silk hats replaced beaver felt in fashion. The mountain men were scattering into new trades: guiding, scouting, army service. Carson's career is the bridge between the trapper era and the emigrant era.

The Donner shadow, two years ahead

In 1846–47, the Donner Party would be trapped by snow near Truckee, north of Carson Pass, with catastrophic loss. The contrast is instructive: Frémont's 1844 party crossed in even deeper winter and lost no one — a difference of leadership, local knowledge, luck, and the fact that they were lean, mounted professionals, not families in wagons.

Whose route was it?

The pass was never “discovered” in any honest sense. Washoe and Northern Sierra Miwok peoples had used and maintained this crossing as a trade route for millennia — by some accounts 5,000 to 10,000 years. The 1844 expedition was shown the way by Native knowledge, then warned against using it in winter. Both facts belong in the story.

Chapter Five

Fame, war, and a continent redrawn

Frémont's published report of the 1843–44 expedition made “Kit Carson” a household name. Then the dime novels took over. Cheap, lurid paperbacks turned the quiet scout into a superhuman Indian fighter slaying dozens single-handedly. Carson, who had to have the stories read aloud to him, was embarrassed by them. Meeting a woman in the East who gushed over meeting the great hero of the novels, he reportedly tried to explain that most of it simply was not true.

The third expedition and war

In 1845 Frémont led a third expedition to California, with Carson again as guide — officially a surveying party, in practice a force positioned for the conflict everyone saw coming. When war between the United States and Mexico erupted in 1846, Frémont and Carson were swept into the conquest of California: the Bear Flag episode, service under Commodore Stockton, and then a march south with General Stephen Kearny's Army of the West, which Carson had guided from New Mexico.

At San Pasqual, near San Diego in December 1846, Kearny's exhausted force was mauled by Californio lancers. Carson was among the men who slipped through enemy lines at night — in one of the era's most retold episodes, crawling barefoot over rocky ground after losing his moccasins — to bring help from San Diego. California was secured for the United States; Carson carried dispatches east to Washington, meeting President Polk. Within months of the war's end, gold was found at Coloma, and the world Frémont and Carson had crossed in silence filled with hundreds of thousands of people.

The road they opened

In the summer of 1848, veterans of the Mormon Battalion heading east from California blazed a wagon road over Carson Pass, following the old Native trade route west down what is now the Highway 88 corridor and the Mormon Emigrant Trail. The Carson Trail became one of the principal Gold Rush routes into California — by some local accounts, a quarter-million travelers used the Carson Pass corridor in the rush years. Every emigrant who sweated up that grade was following, knowingly or not, the line of the 1844 winter crossing.

Chapter Six

The harder second half — and an honest reckoning

A true story does not stop at the heroic crossing. Carson settled in Taos, New Mexico, married Josefa Jaramillo, raised a family, and served from 1853 as a federal Indian agent — a role in which he often argued, in writing, that Native peoples were being cheated and provoked, and that the government broke its own promises.

During the Civil War he became a Union officer in New Mexico. Then, in 1863–64, under orders from his commander, he led the campaign that forced the surrender of the Navajo (Diné) — a scorched-earth operation that destroyed crops, orchards, and livestock and ended in the Long Walk: thousands of Diné marched hundreds of miles to imprisonment at Bosque Redondo, where many died. Carson executed the orders; historians still argue over his reluctance, his responsibility, and his attempts to resign. What is not arguable is the suffering, or that Diné people remember this chapter as defining — the mirror image of the dime-novel hero.

Both things are the record: the scout whose skill saved an expedition in 1844, and the colonel whose campaign devastated a nation in 1864. Carson himself died in 1868 at Fort Lyon, Colorado, at fifty-eight — a month after Josefa's death — reportedly with the words “Adiós, compadres.” Modern historians, and the Washoe, Miwok, and Diné descendants of the people in this story, ask us to hold the whole of it. The pass keeps his name. The story should keep its complexity.

Epilogue

Standing on the pass today

Highway 88 is now one of California's great mountain drives — an all-year, plowed crossing and, at 8,574 feet, the highest Sierra pass kept open in winter. From Fiddletown it is a straight run up Amador County's spine into the story. Places along the way that carry the 1844 expedition with them:

  • Carson Pass summit — Hwy 88The Carson Pass Information Station (seasonal), Pacific Crest Trail crossing, and the Kit Carson Marker, California Historical Landmark No. 315. Stand here in February wind and the 1844 decision stops being abstract.
  • Red Lake & Red Lake PeakImmediately east of the summit. The lake Frémont's men camped by in deep snow, and the peak Frémont and Preuss climbed on Feb. 14, 1844, for the first recorded European-descent sighting of Lake Tahoe.
  • Caples LakeJust west of the pass — the high lake country the party descended through on snowshoes, now a quiet reservoir shoreline under Round Top.
  • Hope Valley & the Carson RiverThe broad, aspen-filled valley on the east side where the expedition turned west, and the river Frémont named for his guide. In October it is one of the Sierra's great fall-color shows.
  • Silver Lake & the old emigrant gradeWest down Highway 88, the corridor of the 1848 Carson Trail — the wagon road that turned a desperate winter trace into the Gold Rush's front door to Amador and El Dorado counties.
  • Cook's Station & Ham's StationHistoric stage and highway stops on the climb from Amador County — reminders that for a century after Carson, this road was worked by stages, freight wagons, and finally automobiles, one hard mile at a time.

Next time you crest the pass — on a drive, on skis, or coasting down the west side the way a certain tandem route now imagines it — it's worth a pause at the summit sign. Under the plowed road lies a Washoe trade route thousands of years old, a February trace broken by starving men on snowshoes, and a wagon road that carried a gold rush. Kit Carson's name is on the sign. The whole layered story is in the ground beneath it.
